description: What a material *is*, declared once so that a recipe can ask for a kind of stuff rather than for a list of species. The companion to growth_forms.json and clades.json: those say what a plant and an animal are, this says what they give up. A recipe naming `#fibre` is satisfied by any material carrying the class, so canon can gain a new reed in ten years' time and every cordage recipe written today accepts it without an edit.
note: Borrowed, deliberately, from the item-tag system Minecraft data packs use -- `#minecraft:planks` rather than an enumeration of nine woods. The argument is the same one and it is about maintenance rather than elegance: canon holds 347 species, and a recipe layer that has to name them is editable for about a month. This is not `flora.uses`, which answers a different question and stays where it is. `uses` says what people do with a plant -- shade, a boundary marker, a landmark to steer by -- and over half of those are not substances at all. A material class says what you can carry away.

fibre.label: Fibre
fibre.note: Anything that can be retted, combed and spun. Plant and animal both -- reed, palm husk, cliff-goat hair -- because a rope does not care which it came from and every recipe that wants one wants either.

timber.label: Timber
timber.note: Wood cut for structure. The distinction from `fuel` is what it is cut *for*: iron-teak is timber and mangrove charcoal is fuel, and the same tree can give both.

bone.label: Bone
bone.note: Bone, antler, tooth and ivory. Canon's leviathans are the reason this is not folded into `stone` as a hard-workable: a bone plate is harvested and a flint is quarried, and the two reach a workshop by entirely different routes.

hide.label: Hide
hide.note: Skin, leather and sinew. Sinew sits here rather than in `fibre` because it is won by skinning, not by retting -- provenance decides the class where the finished behaviour is ambiguous.

shell.label: Shell
shell.note: Mollusc, ammonite and crustacean armour. Canon leans on this hard: the Chess of Fate is inlaid with fossilised ammonites, and the Shattered Sea Oyster is the whole reason Dwarka has a harbour worth the name.

resin.label: Resin
resin.note: Gum, pitch, incense and lac. Frankincense and myrrh are both in canon already as traded scrub, and a resin is the only adhesive this era has.

clay.label: Clay
clay.note: Earth that fires. Held apart from `stone` because the process is the point -- clay is the one material in this list that is *made* hard rather than found hard.

stone.label: Stone
stone.note: Rock worked by knapping, grinding or dressing. Basalt, flint, chert, sandstone.

glass.label: Glass
glass.note: Fused silica, whether a kiln did it or the ground did. Canon's magma-glass and the Glass Scar at Dwarka are natural; a bead is not. Same class, because they knap and cut the same way.

metal.label: Metal
metal.note: Copper, tin, bronze, gold, meteoric iron. The era's outer edge -- canon is a bronze world with iron as a rumour, and nothing in this vocabulary should let a recipe quietly invent a smelted iron industry.

salt.label: Salt
salt.note: Salt, natron and the mineral crusts. Its own class rather than a `physic` or a `produce` because in this world it is a preservative, a trade currency and the ground Dwarka stands on, and all three matter.

pigment.label: Pigment
pigment.note: Dye, ochre, ink and lime-white. Canon has two indigos and grows them on purpose.

grain.label: Grain
grain.note: Staple seed -- rice, barley, millet. Separated from `produce` because grain stores and produce does not, which is the difference a settlement is built on.

produce.label: Produce
produce.note: Fruit, root, leaf and nut eaten as they are. Dates, taro, tamarind.

flesh.label: Flesh
flesh.note: Meat, fish and eggs. Named plainly rather than as `meat` so that fish and shellfish are obviously inside it -- a river culture eats far more of the second than the first.

milk.label: Milk
milk.note: Milk and what sets from it, taken from a living animal. Its own class rather than a `flesh` or an `oil`, and the distinction is the one this game is built on: `flesh` is "meat, fish and eggs" and every one of those ends an animal, where a milking leaves it standing and lets you come back tomorrow. That is the difference between a take and a harvest, and it is why milk is the material a wandering animal can give. `oil` is the pressed and rendered half -- seed oil and fat -- which is a thing done to a body rather than a thing a body offers.

oil.label: Oil
oil.note: Pressed seed oil and rendered fat. Burns, cooks, and waterproofs, which is three recipes' worth of reason to exist. Canon's mahua is already recorded as an oil tree.

fuel.label: Fuel
fuel.note: Charcoal, dung, dry reed and peat. What a process consumes rather than what it transforms -- a firing recipe wants `#fuel` and does not care which.

physic.label: Physic
physic.note: Medicinal substance -- salve, tonic, bitter bark. Canon already carries neem, a wound salve on the myrrh-thorn and a shilajit tonic, so the class is describing what is there rather than proposing a healing system. Nothing in the game reads it as a stat.

spice.label: Spice
spice.note:
Carried in small amounts and worth far more than its weight. Its own class rather than a `produce` for the same reason `salt` is not one: three cardamom pods scent a whole pot, which makes a spice a thing you trade across a continent where produce is a thing you eat where it grew. Added when ginger, mustard and cardamom arrived and `produce` was plainly the wrong word for all three.

Not to be confused with the `seasoning` *use* in plant_uses.json -- that says what people do with a plant, this says what you can carry away. The first draft of the spice materials used `seasoning` here and the lint refused it, which is the entire reason both pins exist.

poison.label: Poison
poison.note:
A substance known to harm, and gathered on purpose. Its own class rather than a bitter `physic`, because a household that keeps kuchla in a sealed jar is not keeping medicine and knows it.

**Nothing can be made of it except medicine, and that is the vocabulary working rather than a gap.** `affordances.json` has no word for harm -- it was written that way so the cozy ruling could not be quietly undone -- so an object made to poison somebody could not say what it was for. Canon therefore records the stuff and stops: the only recipes that consume a poison are the ones that purify it. That is also, as it happens, what the tradition these plants come from actually does.
